newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-CAN ANYBODY KEEP CONTROL AT BAYERN MUNICH?.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CAN ANYBODY KEEP CONTROL AT BAYERN MUNICH?.

text.p: After a rare public display of anger from striker Juergen Klinsmann and more harsh words from chairman Franz Beckenbauer, many German soccer experts are asking one question as the Bundesliga title race begins the final three games.
Is it possible for anyone to keep control at Bayern Munich anymore?

Bayern, who have won the German championship just twice in the 1990s after dominating the Bundesliga for much of the previous two decades, have a one-point lead over rivals Bayer Leverkusen before they visit lowly Hansa Rostock on Friday.

But the Bavarians seem to have lost their nerves completely after a poor goalless draw at home with relegated Freiburg last weekend when an angry Klinsmann kicked a hole in an advertising sign after he was substituted.
After the match chairman Beckenbauer, who has become more and more critical of the team recently, said the club had "no chance" of winning the title in that form.
Former coach Udo Lattek, who guided Bayern through some of the best days of the club's history in the 1970s, thinks Leverkusen are now favourites to win their first ever championship.
"Especially since Bayern have started all that drama just at the 'right' moment," Lattek said. "This weekend is going to be a crunch weekend in my opinion...There is no harmony in this Bayern team."
Anybody who has watched national team captain Klinsmann in training knows that he can be temperamental.

In the past Klinsmann has been seen storming away from the training pitch in anger. But the veteran striker usually appears from the shower talking sweetly and diplomatically about his team mates and coach to the media.

This public display of frustration before a capacity 63,000 crowd, however, shows that the player still has major problems with the atmosphere at Bayern even though he has less than a month to endure before he leaves the club.

The general internal squabbling in Bayern's dressing rooms is believed to go much further. Beckenbauer, who has high profile jobs in the German media as well as at Bayern, does not seem to be helping matters by attacking the team in public.
The whole situation is putting extra pressure on coach Giovanni Trapattoni who must be tempted to take up the offers he has received to return to his native Italy.

Bayern have been through some top-class coaches in recent years without much success. With so many leading figures in both the team and the boardroom, it seems an almost impossible job for any trainer to keep a grip.

Leverkusen coach Christoph Daum, who guided VfB Stuttgart to the title in 1992 and is regarded as one of the great motivators in the game, needs only to show his team the Munich newspapers to persuade them that they can snatch the title.

Leverkusen, who seem to have an easier run-in than Bayern, take on relegation candidates St Pauli at home on Saturday. If they win and Bayern slip up at Rostock, Daum may be looking at another great triumph.
